newsitem.title: LITHUANIA: Lithuania seen luring Baltic banks eventually.
newsitem.headline: Lithuania seen luring Baltic banks eventually.

text.p: Estonian and Latvian banks might spearhead a foreign drive into Lithuania as the banking sector recovers from a crisis that rocked its foundations, analysts say.

The first cross border move among Baltic banks was in early 1996 when Estonia's largest bank, Hansapank, bought Latvian bank Deutsch-Lettische Bank. So far none has ventured into the Lithuanian market and taken significant stakes.

"It's only a matter of time," said Tomas Lind, senior area manager for Swedish commercial bank S-E-Banken covering the Baltic countries. "It's difficult for the largest banks in Estonia to have any significant growth on the Estonia market."

"The way to grow would be to invest into the other two countries which makes sense given the experience the Estonian banks have had of building up their operations in their own countries," Lind told Reuters.
The Estonian banking market is much farther advanced than Latvia's or Lithuania's.
As the dust settles from the crisis of end-1995 which disrupted the development of Lithuania's infant banking sector, two clear winners have pulled to the forefront, Vilniaus and Hermis.

Analysts named Estonia's Hansapank and Hoiupank and Latvia's Unibanka as likely candidates to move into the Lithuanian market benefiting from new laws which have made it easier for foreign banks to set up operations.
"The Lithuanian market was somewhat restricted in terms of foreign investment until sometime last year. They have now opened their doors," Lind said.

Hansapank has set up leasing operations in Lithuania and Hoiupank will probably be interested in Lithuania's commercial market because it has the largest population of the Baltic countries, analysts say.

"Hansapank has been the single most aggressive bank and I would imagine that they would either try to acquire or invest in a bank, starting from zero, in Lithuania," said Bo Kragh, area manager for Baltic financial institutions at Sweden's Handelsbanken.

"Lithuania had its banking crisis first of the three countries and it's not over yet. This leads to a situation where newcomers can be welcome and prices of existing banks can be low," Kragh told Reuters.
Russian and Polish markets would be a bit too big for Baltic banks to take on, while Estonia is too small, Kragh said.
"Hansapank has already said it has limited scope for expansion in its own country. So Lithuania would be the obvious match," Kragh said.

Poland's Kredyt Bank has received permission to set up operations in Lithuania and Latvia's Saules Bank, which is 20 percent owned by Tallinna Pank, is establishing leasing options and other banking activities in Lithuania.

The Lithuanian government said it would close two of the country's top banks, Litimpeks and Innovation, as part of a campaign to restore shaken consumer confidence in the system since the banking crisis.
Litimpeks has since been reopened but Innovation will be liquidated and its depositors compensated at an estimated cost of 350 million litas.
Two of the country's three big state banks, the Agriculture Bank and the State Commercial Bank, are slated to be privatised this year.
Some concern remains for the fledgling Lithuanian market, with some analysts saying it is still crippled by the lack of a functioning inter-bank market.
Lithuania's central bank has said it would try to remedy the situation and to help ease liquidity problems by beginning monthly repurchase tenders in April.
